clue.text: Rejection of deal about Northern Ireland

indicators.note: one word placed about another wraps around it, so the abbreviation sits inside the word for a hand of cards

parts.note: taken as written: a hand dealt at cards
NI is the standard abbreviation for Northern Ireland

explanation.surface: A political deal over Northern Ireland is rejected by one side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deal' reads as an agreement to be rejected, but it is the outer shell, opened up around the abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A denial is a refusal to accept something, which is a rejection.

clue.text: Girl right at all times

parts.note: Eve, a girl's name
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A girl who is always right.
explanation.walkthrough: EVE + R gives EVER.
explanation.definitionFit: Ever means always, at every moment, as in 'ever vigilant'.

clue.text: Watered land to prepare tiger-raid

indicators.note: to prepare something is to make it ready, working the raw material into a new form

parts.note: taken as written, every letter used

explanation.surface: Farmers water their land to get ready for a tiger attack.
explanation.walkthrough: The scan reads 'tiger-maid', but the letters need two Rs and no M; 'tiger-raid' is the printed word misread, and it rearranges exactly.
explanation.definitionFit: To irrigate is to supply land with water by channels, so irrigated means watered land, as a verb phrase.

clue.text: Wash involving no toil

indicators.note: to involve originally means to wrap or entangle, so the letters are twisted up together

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A laundry promise: washing that involves no hard work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wash' looks like laundry, but it is the noun for a liquid applied to the skin.
explanation.definitionFit: A wash is a medicated liquid for bathing a part of the body, which is what a lotion is.

clue.text: Dry ore is somehow ridiculous

indicators.note: somehow says the letters get there by some unstated means, so their order is not to be trusted

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written; the word does double work as fodder

explanation.surface: Someone scoffs that calling ore dry is a silly thing to say.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of DRY ORE IS rearrange to DERISORY; the fodder runs right up to the indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: Derisory means so small or poor as to deserve mockery, hence laughable or ridiculous.

clue.text: Girl-architect a man may have to watch?

definitions.text: Girl-architect a man may have to watch?

parts.note: the surface reading: a woman who draws up building plans

parts.words: a man may have to watch?
parts.note: the setter's reading: a woman with schemes on a man, who should be on his guard

explanation.walkthrough: Designing means drawing plans, as an architect does, but also scheming, which is why a man must watch out.
explanation.definitionFit: A designing woman is a calculating, scheming one, with plans that a man would do well to watch.

clue.text: Rode off after others but made good

indicators.note: after sends the rearranged riding word behind the word for the remainder

parts.note: the rest means the others

indicators.note: off means gone wrong or out of order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A rider chased the others but redeemed himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rode off after others' reads as a chase; 'after' only fixes the order, putting the shuffled riding word second.
explanation.definitionFit: To make good something damaged is to repair or return it to its former state, which is to restore it.

clue.text: It may help drinker with recurring skin trouble

indicators.note: recurring is read as running back again, so the word goes in the opposite direction

parts.note: warts are small growths on the skin

explanation.surface: Something that helps a drinker who suffers from repeated skin problems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recurring' looks medical but turns WARTS round; in a down light it reads upward.
explanation.definitionFit: A straw is a thin tube for sucking up a drink, which helps a drinker.

clue.text: Two men changing coats at meeting

parts.note: first man: Roy

indicators.note: changing says the following letters alter their arrangement

parts.note: second man: Al
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Two men swap jackets at a gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Meeting' in racing means a race event; Royal Ascot is the June race meeting in Berkshire attended by the royal family.
explanation.definitionFit: A race meeting is a fixture of horse races, and Royal Ascot is a famous one.

clue.text: Trusted one with mass of rock fragments?

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A reliable person is handed a heap of rubble, as if in reward.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter gives no word telling you to rearrange: the question mark is all the warning there is, so TRUSTED plus I is shuffled into DETRITUS unannounced.
explanation.definitionFit: Detritus is the loose debris worn off rock by weathering, a geologist's word for such accumulated fragments.

clue.text: Way beams find stragglers

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way
beams of light are rays

explanation.surface: Searchlight beams sweep a road looking for people who have fallen behind.
explanation.walkthrough: ST and RAYS join to make STRAYS.
explanation.definitionFit: Strays are those that wander off or lag behind the group, just as stragglers do.

clue.text: He wrote of king or spring

parts.note: George is the name of six British kings
taken as written
a spring is a source of water, as is a well

explanation.surface: A question of whether some author wrote about a monarch or about springtime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring' pushes the season; here it is a water source. GEORGE + OR + WELL gives GEORGE ORWELL.
explanation.definitionFit: George Orwell was the pen name of Eric Blair, novelist of Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four, so he is one who wrote.

clue.text: Gun raised at charge as a rule

indicators.note: raised means lifted upward, and in a down light a word written upward is read backwards

parts.note: the Luger is a German pistol
taken as written
an ion is an atom carrying an electric charge

explanation.surface: Raising a gun when charging is standard practice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As a rule' reads as one idiom meaning usually; here 'as a' only links, and 'rule' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A regulation is an official rule or directive.

clue.text: One in group taking chair

indicators.note: in places the first item inside the second, here a numeral-like word within a word for a collection

parts.note: a set is a group of things that go together
a, the indefinite article, means one

explanation.surface: A member of a committee takes the chair at a meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking chair' looks like chairing a meeting; here A goes into SET to give SEAT.
explanation.definitionFit: A seat is anything to sit on, and a chair is one kind.

clue.text: Catalogue of suggestions for perfectionist, possibly

indicators.note: a catalogue of something names its contents after it, so the contents word comes first in the compound

parts.note: suggestions are ideas, used here in the singular as the first half of a compound
a catalogue is a list

explanation.surface: A fussy perfectionist is handed a catalogue of suggestions for improvement.
explanation.walkthrough: A catalogue of suggestions is an IDEA LIST, run together as IDEALIST; 'possibly' marks the definition as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: An idealist holds to standards of perfection, so a perfectionist may be one, which is why the setter adds a qualifier.

clue.text: Promising youth getting to be fond of lively lady novice

parts.note: to like is to be fond of

indicators.note: lively suggests energetic movement, so the letters jump into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
L is a learner, from the L-plate on a learner driver's car

explanation.surface: A young man of promise grows fond of a spirited young woman who is new to things.
explanation.walkthrough: The novice's L joins LADY before the shuffle. A likely lad is British slang for a lively, promising young man.
explanation.definitionFit: Likely here means showing promise, so a likely lad is a youth who seems bound to do well.

clue.text: Follower of record (LP) that is remarkable

parts.note: a gramophone record is a disc

indicators.note: remarkable is read as re-markable, able to be marked out afresh, so the letters are set down in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: A fan of a remarkable long-playing album.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Follower of record' reads as one phrase; only 'Follower' is the definition. LP stands for long-playing record, but here its two letters are fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A disciple is a devoted adherent of a teacher or cause, someone who follows.

clue.text: Packing up old courting habit

definitions.meaning: first meaning: tying things together into a bundle
second meaning: a historical custom of a courting couple sharing a bed fully clothed

explanation.walkthrough: Bundling was a custom in early New England and Wales: the couple lay together clothed, sometimes with a board between them.
explanation.definitionFit: The same -ing word names wrapping goods into bundles and the old custom of courting couples sharing a bed in their clothes.

clue.text: Bird getting in a tangle

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a wading bird of the sandpiper family
second meaning: a twisted, snarled lump of string or hair

explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a bird caught in netting; the bird and the tangle are two senses of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The knot is a stocky shorebird, and a knot is also an interlaced tangle in thread or hair.

clue.text: Wave making oarsman sick inside

indicators.note: inside places the word for being unwell within the word for a rower

parts.note: bow is the rower seated nearest the front of the boat
ill means sick

explanation.surface: A big wave makes a rower seasick.
explanation.walkthrough: In a rowing crew, 'bow' is the name of the oarsman nearest the bow.
explanation.definitionFit: A billow is a large swelling wave of the sea.

clue.text: Sailor's account for cleaning ship's bottom, perhaps

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the hard-drinking seaman of a bawdy old sea song

definitions.text: account for cleaning ship's bottom, perhaps
definitions.meaning: second meaning, read literally: the invoice for scraping off the shellfish that cling to a hull

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sailor's' reads as possessive, but the 's is just 'is'. The second half is whimsical: a bill for de-barnacling a hull, as 'perhaps' admits.
explanation.definitionFit: Barnacle Bill is the stock name of a sailor from a well-known sea shanty, used jokingly of any old salt.

clue.text: Not by any means a specialised skill, we hear

indicators.note: we hear says the answer is what reaches the ear, not how the clue word is spelt

parts.note: know-how is practical expertise

explanation.surface: A disclaimer that something is in no way a specialist skill.
explanation.walkthrough: Nohow is an informal word for in no way; it sounds just like know-how.
explanation.definitionFit: Nohow is a dialect or informal adverb meaning in no way at all.

clue.text: A convict returning for festive occasion

indicators.note: returning means going back the way it came, so the pair is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written
a lag is British slang for a convict, especially an old lag

explanation.surface: A prisoner comes home for a celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: A LAG read backwards gives GALA.
explanation.definitionFit: A gala is a festive celebration or special entertainment.

clue.text: Man in drink — he's also on the board

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a churchman who also gives his name to a mulled, spiced port
second meaning: a chess piece that moves diagonally

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a drunk company director; the board is the chessboard, and the drink is the hot punch of port, oranges and spice.
explanation.definitionFit: A bishop is a senior cleric, the old name for mulled port, and one of the pieces on a chessboard.

clue.text: Nobody doubting raid is over

definitions.meaning: first meaning, read as two words: everyone is clear on it
second meaning: the siren signal that an air attack has ended

explanation.walkthrough: Split into its two words the phrase means everybody understands; as one phrase it is the wartime signal that the bombers have gone.
explanation.definitionFit: The all-clear is the signal given when danger such as an air raid has passed, and 'all clear' also describes everyone being certain.

clue.text: Year when no precise location indicated

parts.note: the surface reading: someone asking for a date
the setter's reading: a place left unspecified, any place at all

explanation.surface: A record gives a date but no place for some event.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening words supply no letters that we can account for; the answer comes from the definition and the crossing letters alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Anywhere means in or to any place, so it fixes no particular spot.

clue.text: College putting meat roll first

indicators.note: putting one thing first sets the order, sending the meat word second and the bundle word to the front

parts.note: a wad is a roll, as of banknotes
ham is cured pork

explanation.surface: A college kitchen serves a meat roll.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Meat roll' reads as one dish; it is two pieces, and the roll goes in front. Wadham is a college of Oxford University.
explanation.definitionFit: Wadham College is one of the constituent colleges of the University of Oxford, founded in 1610.
